theory.intro: A **conclusion** is a statement about the world that the data gives you a reason to believe. It is **supported** when it stays inside what the data covers and can be backed by the statistics themselves.
facts: A conclusion is supported only when you can quote evidence for it from the data itself.
A conclusion **overreaches** when it makes a claim that the measurements or sampling method do not justify.
Interpret the mean in context: a higher mean is usually better for marks or amounts raised, but a lower mean is better for time taken.
A **smaller range** means greater **consistency**. Use centre and spread together when comparing datasets.
When the two statistics disagree, say so — one dataset can be higher on average while the other is the more consistent.
A **census** collects data from every member of the population, but measurement or recording errors can still occur.

A **sample** can support conclusions about the population when it is appropriately representative. Random selection reduces selection bias but does not guarantee that the sample obtained represents the population.
A sample drawn from one restricted group may not represent the wider population; consider how that group differs from the population.
Observational data can provide evidence about possible causes, but an observed change alone does not establish what caused it. A fair test with a control group can provide stronger evidence.
Past data can inform forecasts, but it does not prove what will happen in the future.
Data alone does not justify a conclusion about something that was never measured.
steps: Name the group and what the data actually measures
Interpret centre and spread in context: decide whether higher or lower values are better and compare consistency
Check whether the measurements and sampling method justify the conclusion
Quote the statistics or sampling evidence that support your answer

foundation.question_text:
The table shows the mean and the range of the amounts, in dollars, raised each week by two Year $8$ fundraising teams over a term.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Team}&\textbf{Mean}&\textbf{Range}\\ \hline \text{Blue}&\$96&\$48\\ \text{Gold}&\$112&\$20\end{array}$
The fundraising trophy goes to the better team.
Which team should get it?
Give two reasons.
foundation.solution_text:
$\$112 > \$96$
Gold has the higher mean, so Gold raised more per week on average.
$\$20 < \$48$
Gold has the smaller range, so Gold was also steadier from week to week.
**Gold should get the trophy**, because both statistics point the same way.

foundation.question_text:
The table shows the mean and the range of the numbers of library books borrowed per student last term by two Year $7$ classes.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Class}&\textbf{Mean}&\textbf{Range}\\ \hline 7\text{A}&14&9\\ 7\text{B}&17&22\end{array}$
Ravi says that $7$B is the better borrowing class in every way.
Is Ravi correct?
Use both statistics in your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
$17 > 14$
$7$B has the higher mean, so $7$B borrowed more books per student on average.
$9 < 22$
$7$A has the smaller range, so $7$A's students were much more alike in how much they borrowed.
**Ravi is not correct**: the data supports $7$B being ahead on average, but $7$A is the more consistent class.

foundation.question_text:
The table shows summary information about a class's test marks in three subjects.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Subject}&\textbf{Median mark}&\textbf{Range of marks}\\ \hline \text{English}&62&28\\ \text{Maths}&68&41\\ \text{Science}&65&19\end{array}$
In which subject did students do best?
In which subject were their marks most similar?
Use the statistics to explain your answers.
foundation.solution_text:
$68 > 65 > 62$
Students did best in maths, which has the highest median mark of $68$.
$19 < 28 < 41$
Their marks were most similar in science, which has the smallest range of $19$.

foundation.question_text:
The SRC asked the $24$ students in one Year $7$ class which day the sports carnival should be held.
$15$ of them chose Friday, so the SRC concluded that most of the $900$ students in the school want Friday.
Is this conclusion supported by the data?
Explain.
foundation.solution_text:
The data describes only the $24$ students in that one class.
Those $24$ students are a sample of the $900$, and one Year $7$ class cannot speak for every year group in the school.
**Not supported** — the data supports a conclusion about that class only.

foundation.question_text:
Posters about recycling were put up in a school.
In the four weeks before the posters went up, a mean of $42$ drink bottles per day were placed in the recycling bins.
In the four weeks after, the mean was $58$ per day.
Mia concludes that the posters caused the increase.
Is her conclusion supported by the data?
Explain.
foundation.solution_text:
The data shows that the mean rose from $42$ to $58$ bottles per day, so it does support the conclusion that more bottles were recycled after the posters went up.
Nothing was recorded about **why** the number rose — warmer weather, a new bin position or a class competition would explain it just as well.
**Not supported** — the data shows what changed, not what caused the change.

development.question_text:
The table shows the mean and the range of the numbers of books borrowed each week from three sections of a school library over a term.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Section}&\textbf{Mean}&\textbf{Range}\\ \hline \text{Fiction}&84&31\\ \text{Non-fiction}&62&12\\ \text{Graphic}&79&45\end{array}$
Write a conclusion about which section is borrowed from most, and a separate conclusion about which section's borrowing is steadiest.
Quote the statistics you use.
development.solution_text:
$84 > 79 > 62$
Fiction has the greatest mean, so fiction is the section borrowed from most, at about $84$ books each week.
$12 < 31 < 45$
Non-fiction has the smallest range, so non-fiction borrowing is the steadiest from week to week.
The two conclusions describe different things, so both can be true at the same time.

development.question_text:
The table shows summary information about the times, in seconds, taken by four age groups to complete a puzzle.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Age (years)}&\textbf{Mean (seconds)}&\textbf{Range (seconds)}\\ \hline 12\text{–}16&26.4&17.5\\ 16\text{–}30&24.8&14.2\\ 30\text{–}60&32.1&20.6\\ \text{Over }60&43.7&10.8\end{array}$
Noah thinks the over $60$s did best because they have the greatest mean.
Explain why Noah is not correct.
Put the age groups in order from most consistent to least consistent.
development.solution_text:
A lower mean time is better because it means finishing the puzzle faster.
The over $60$s have the highest mean time, $43.7$ seconds, so they took the longest on average. The $16$–$30$ group was fastest on average, with a mean of $24.8$ seconds.
$10.8 < 14.2 < 17.5 < 20.6$
From most consistent to least consistent: over $60$, $16$–$30$, $12$–$16$, $30$–$60$.

development.question_text:
Every student in class $8$C was asked how many hours they spent on their class science project.
The mean was $4.2$ hours.
The school newsletter reports that 'students at this school spend about $4.2$ hours on their projects'.
Explain what is wrong with the newsletter's conclusion, and write a corrected version.
development.solution_text:
Only the students in $8$C were asked, so the data describes $8$C and no one else.
Every other class in the school was left out, and their projects may take a very different amount of time.
**The newsletter's conclusion overreaches**, because it stretches one class's result to the whole school.
A corrected version is 'students in $8$C spend about $4.2$ hours on their class science project'.

development.question_text:
A school wants to investigate whether its $640$ students would use a new bike rack.
A group asks $30$ students standing at the existing bike racks after school, and $28$ say they would use it.
Explain why this sampling method may give an unrepresentative sample of the school.
development.solution_text:
The group asks only students standing at the existing bike racks after school.
These students may be more likely to ride to school and want a new bike rack than other students.
Students who are not at the bike racks are excluded, so the $28$ yes responses out of $30$ may not represent the preferences of all $640$ students.

development.question_text:
The table shows the mean and the range of the amounts, in dollars, taken each hour by three stalls at a school fete, over the six hours the fete was open.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Stall}&\textbf{Mean}&\textbf{Range}\\ \hline \text{Cakes}&\$58&\$22\\ \text{Drinks}&\$71&\$46\\ \text{Books}&\$44&\$9\end{array}$
Write two conclusions this table supports, and explain why 'the drinks stall was the best stall' is not one of them.
development.solution_text:
$\$71 > \$58 > \$44$
The drinks stall has the greatest mean, so it took the most money per hour on average, about $\$71$.
$\$9 < \$22 < \$46$
The books stall has the smallest range, so its takings were the steadiest across the six hours.
'Best' has not been defined, and the two statistics point to different stalls, so the table on its own does not support calling any one stall the best.

mastery.question_text:
For one term the SRC weighed the paper recycled each week by two year groups.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Year}&\textbf{Mean (kg)}&\textbf{Range (kg)}\\ \hline 7&18.4&6.2\\ 10&21.5&15.8\end{array}$
Compare the amounts recycled by Year $7$ and Year $10$, using both statistics to explain your answer.
mastery.solution_text:
$21.5 > 18.4$
Year $10$ has the higher mean, so Year $10$ recycled more paper per week on average.
$6.2 < 15.8$
Year $7$ has the smaller range, so Year $7$ was more consistent from week to week.
Year $10$ recycled more on average, while Year $7$ recycled a steadier amount.

mastery.question_text:
The table shows summary information about the times, in minutes, taken by two groups to complete a test.
$\begin{array}{lccc}\textbf{Group}&\textbf{Mean}&\textbf{Median}&\textbf{Range}\\ \hline \text{A}&29.65&29.5&8.4\\ \text{B}&28.90&28.7&11.2\end{array}$
Compare the two groups' completion times, referring to their mean, median and range.
mastery.solution_text:
$28.90 < 29.65$ and $28.7 < 29.5$
Group B finished faster on average: its mean and median times are both lower.
$8.4 < 11.2$
Group A was more consistent because its completion times have the smaller range.
Group B was faster on average, while Group A's times were more consistent.

mastery.question_text:
A school wants to investigate how many books its $700$ students read last month, including books from the school library and elsewhere.
Ben asks the first $50$ students who walk out of the library, and their mean is $7.2$ books.
Explain why Ben's sampling method may produce an unrepresentative sample.
mastery.solution_text:
Ben selects students leaving the library and excludes students who do not visit it at that time.
Those selected students may have different reading habits from other students, so their mean of $7.2$ books may not represent the school. The data does not prove that this mean is too high.
